title: Immigration Court Memo Cuts Key Filing Deadlines to 10 Days
excerpt: EOIR's Policy Memorandum 27-02, effective November 23, replaces month-long and 60-day filing windows with 10-day deadlines for represented respondents in removal cases.
body:
• A new EOIR policy memo, effective November 23, 2026, cuts the deadline to file written pleadings and evidence on removability to 10 days from a judge's scheduling order — down from about a month under the 2021 guidance it replaces.
  • Applications for relief or protection, with supporting documents, are also due 10 days after a judge sustains the charges of removability — down from 60 days.
  • The model applies to represented respondents: if a lawyer files Form EOIR-28 at least 15 days before a master calendar hearing, that hearing is vacated and the case proceeds on written deadlines instead.
  • Miss a deadline and the consequences are written into the memo: DHS may ask the judge to find removability and issue a final order, and an unfiled application is deemed waived.

People fighting removal in US immigration court who have a lawyer now face far shorter filing deadlines. A policy memorandum issued by the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) on November 23 — Policy Memorandum 27-02, signed by Acting Director Sirce Owen — replaces the Biden-era case-flow guidance with a model built around written filings and 10-day deadlines, Bloomberg Law reported.

Who is affected

The new model covers removal cases in which the respondent has a representative — a lawyer or accredited representative who files Form EOIR-28, the notice of appearance. Where the representative files that form at least 15 days before a master calendar hearing, the hearing will be vacated and the court will instead send both sides a scheduling order setting the filing deadlines.

If the form is filed less than 15 days before the hearing, or at the hearing itself, the respondent and representative must still appear. The memo applies prospectively to cases initiated on or after November 23, 2026; pending cases may be added to the model only after an individual determination that they are suited to it, and existing court orders stay in effect unless a judge changes them.

What changed, precisely

Under the 2021 guidance the memo cancels, respondents had about a month from a judge's scheduling order to file written pleadings and evidence on the charges of removability, and 60 days to file applications for relief or protection after being found removable. The new deadlines are counted in calendar days; a deadline falling on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday moves to the next business day.

After pleadings and removability evidence are filed, the other side has 20 days to respond. The judge then decides removability on the papers, orders more briefing or evidence, or schedules a hearing — and issues a written determination if the case is decided on filings. Cases found trial-ready go into a trial queue for a merits hearing within 90 days, subject to docket availability, and amendments or supplemental filings are due at least 10 days before that hearing.

What to do next

The practical change is timing, and it starts before any deadline is set. Filing Form EOIR-28 at least 15 days before a master calendar hearing is what moves a case into the written track, so representation needs to be in place early. Evidence on removability, and later the relief application with its supporting documents — which can include country-conditions evidence — must be ready to file within days of the court's orders, not weeks.

The deadlines are not absolute: the memo notes that parties may request a master calendar hearing or ask a judge, by written motion, to extend a filing deadline or accept a late filing. Judges also keep discretion to use scheduling orders outside this model.

What happens if they do nothing

If written pleadings are not filed on time, the Department of Homeland Security may proceed by written motion to ask the court to find removability and issue a final order. If DHS fails to meet its own burden on removability, the respondent may move to terminate. And if an application or document is not filed within the time the judge sets, the opportunity to file it is deemed waived under the regulation the memo cites, 8 C.F.R. § 1003.31(c).

EOIR's stated reason for the change is docket efficiency: in many represented cases, the agency says, removability is not contested and initial hearings are held only to take pleadings and set deadlines — work it argues can be done on paper, freeing hearing time for contested cases.
